title: Humanoid Robots Move Beyond Dancing to Real-World Firefighting at Beijing Games
excerpt: The 2nd World Humanoid Robot Games will feature 50 events across five days, with robots competing in real-world scenarios including firefighting, retail and factory work.
body:
• The 2nd World Humanoid Robot Games will run August 22-26 in Beijing with 50 events, up from 26 in the inaugural 2025 edition, including new real-world scenario-based competitions.
  • Robots will compete in actual factories, hotels and homes rather than simulated arenas, performing tasks like firefighting, clothes folding and food preparation.
  • The 100-meter race has been upgraded to fully autonomous robots only, and a new dexterous-hand competition will test micro-level manipulation across eight high-precision tasks.

When the first World Humanoid Robot Games were held in Beijing last August, the spectacle of 500 robots from 16 countries attempting athletic feats drew 1.33 billion media views — and no small amount of amusement, as the machines stumbled, crashed and generally evoked what one observer described as "drunks stumbling into each other."

The second edition, scheduled for August 22-26 at Beijing's National Speed Skating Oval, aims to change that narrative. With 50 events across five days — nearly double the inaugural lineup — organizers are shifting the competition from choreographed demonstrations toward proving that humanoid robots can perform useful work in real environments.

From Test Arenas to Real Workplaces

The most significant change is that scenario-based competitions will no longer take place in purpose-built test arenas. Instead, robots will operate in actual factories, hotels and model homes, where they must autonomously complete complex, long-duration tasks with tangible outputs.

https://x.com/PDChina/status/2089245847058076087

New events test skills directly relevant to commercial deployment: folding clothes in home settings, firefighting in emergency rescue scenarios, preparing food in retail environments, and completing full workflows in factory and logistics operations. More than 40 percent of this year's events are application-focused scenario contests, according to Liu Weiliang, deputy director of the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Economy and Information Technology.

"The ultimate goal is to enable robots to receive orders through competition and take up jobs after the games."

— Liu Weiliang, Beijing Municipal Bureau of Economy and Information Technology

Greater Autonomy, Greater Dexterity

The competitive bar has been raised across the board. The signature 100-meter race has been upgraded to a fully autonomous event — no remote control allowed. Robot soccer players are now capable of dribbling while in motion and making diving saves, with officials expecting competitive skill levels to advance from "preschooler" to "youth" stage.

A new dexterous-hand competition makes its debut, featuring eight high-precision tasks including power tool assembly, powder weighing and bottle opening. A ping-pong competition, organized by the Hitch Open Ping-Pong Embodied AI Challenge, will also join the official lineup, turning one of the world's fastest sports into a proving ground for robotic perception and movement.

The Gap Between Hype and Reality

The games arrive at a moment of both extraordinary ambition and sober reality checks for China's robotics industry. Beijing's five-year economic blueprint through 2030 elevated robotics to an essential growth driver, and authorities have allocated at least $20 billion in subsidies since 2024, according to Reuters. Investment in robotics and embodied AI reached 73.5 billion yuan ($10.8 billion) in 2025 alone.

But a Reuters analysis cautioned that a "yawning gap between hype and reality" persists. Chinese officials issued a rare warning in November about the risks of a bubble forming, pointing to some 150 humanoid manufacturers overcrowding the market. More than 450,000 firms were registered in intelligent robotics by the end of 2024, triple the number four years earlier.

Some companies are already demonstrating commercial traction. Robotera, a Beijing-based startup, says its robots have been deployed at China Post and SF Express logistics centers across multiple regions, reaching roughly 85 percent of human-level efficiency while operating around the clock.

What's Next

Organizers have invited potential commercial customers — factories, hotels, universities and tourism operators — to attend the event, with dedicated meeting spaces set up for direct discussions between developers and clients. The goal is explicit: translate competition medals into commercial orders, creating an ecosystem where proving grounds become sales floors.
